title: Matthew 9:18–26
context: While Jesus teaches, a ruler kneels for his dead daughter; on the way, a woman with a twelve-year hemorrhage touches His fringe and is healed. At the house, mockery yields to Jesus’ hand, and the girl arises—twin mercies of interrupted journey and restored life.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Older voices from both traditions on Matthew 9:18–26.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Just dead - He had left her at the point of death, Mark v, 23. Probably a messenger had now informed him she was dead. Coming behind - Out of bashfulness and humility. Take courage - Probably she was struck with fear, when he turned and looked upon her, Mark v, 33; Luke viii, 47; lest she should have offended him, by touching his garment privately; and the more so, because she was unclean according to the law, Lev. xv, 25.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 9:18–26)

reformed.quote: While he was speaking these things to them. Those who imagine that the narrative, which is here given by Mark and Luke, is different from that of Matthew, are so clearly refuted by the passage itself, that there is no necessity for a lengthened debate.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 9:18–26)

verses.text: While he told these things to them, behold, a ruler came and worshiped him, saying, “My daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live.”
verses.arminianNotes:
A ruler interrupts teaching with worshipful kneeling and daring faith: touch her, and she will live—even after death. Desperation becomes trust.

Come as you are, with the need you cannot fix. Grace meets faith that asks Jesus to act. The plea is personal and hopeful, not presumptuous magic.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Behold” again: authority figures kneel. Faith names Jesus’ hand as life’s instrument after death has spoken.

Such trust is gift. The ruler’s words rest on Christ’s power under the Father’s will. Death is not final where the Lord of life is present.

verses.text: Jesus got up and followed him, as did his disciples.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus rises and goes. The Teacher becomes the companion of grief. Disciples learn mercy by walking toward a death-house.

The Savior is willing. He does not delay behind excuses; He follows need. Both hear: compassion in motion.
verses.reformedNotes:
The King accompanies the request. Disciples are drawn into His path of mercy.

Providence includes this detour that will double as miracle for a bleeding woman and a dead child.

verses.text: Behold, a woman who had a discharge of blood for twelve years came behind him, and touched the fringe of his garment;
verses.arminianNotes:
Twelve years of uncleanness and isolation; she approaches from behind—ashamed yet believing. The fringe of the garment is enough if Jesus is who He is.

Chronic suffering can still reach for Christ. Faith may be trembling and quiet; it is still faith that comes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Hidden misery meets holy fringe. Levitical uncleanness sought the Holy One without announcement.

No years of bleeding outrun Christ’s reach. The approach itself is ordered under mercy.

verses.text: for she said within herself, “If I just touch his garment, I will be made well.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Inner speech of faith: contact with Jesus means wellness. She reasons from who He is to what He can do.

Arminians honor this responsible trust. She acts on conviction grace has awakened. Minimal contact, maximal confidence in Him—not in technique.
verses.reformedNotes:
Faith speaks before lips do. “I will be made well” rests on Christ’s sufficiency.

Saving and healing trust are God-wrought. Her resolve does not create power; it receives the One who has it.

verses.text: But Jesus, turning around and seeing her, said, “Daughter, cheer up! Your faith has made you well.” And the woman was made well from that hour.
verses.arminianNotes:
He turns, sees, and names her “daughter”—public honor for private faith. “Your faith has made you well” (literally saved/healed) ties her trust to His gift; healing is instant.

Faith is the appointed means of receiving mercy. Jesus affirms her trust without flattering her strength. He is the healer; faith is the empty hand.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jesus will not leave her anonymous. Daughter-language adopts; faith-language explains the instrument, not the ultimate cause.

“Your faith has made you well” means faith as God-given channel, not autonomous force. Instant healing seals the word of the Son.
verses.keyContrast: Both honor the woman’s faith and Christ’s power. Arminians stress faith as grace-enabled means that truly receives; Reformed commentators underline that even this faith is gift, while Christ alone effects the healing.

verses.text: When Jesus came into the ruler’s house and saw the flute players and the crowd in noisy disorder,
verses.arminianNotes:
Professional mourning is already underway—death treated as settled. Noise fills the house where Jesus intends life.

Culture’s verdict is not final. Do not let commotion drown the Lord’s arrival.
verses.reformedNotes:
Funeral liturgy meets the Lord of the living. The scene is set for unbelief’s laugh.

Human certainty about death will be overturned by the One who commands.

verses.text: he said to them, “Make room, because the girl isn’t dead, but sleeping.” They were ridiculing him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus reframes death as sleep under His authority. The crowd laughs—faithlessness as mockery.

Ridicule often greets hope. Keep company with Jesus’ word, not the laugh track of despair.
verses.reformedNotes:
Sleep is death’s temporary name when Christ is present. Their laughter judges them.

He speaks reality they cannot see. Resurrection power is already implied in His speech.

verses.text: But when the crowd was sent out, he entered in, took her by the hand, and the girl arose.
verses.arminianNotes:
Mockers expelled; Jesus takes her hand; she arises. Touch and life again—gentle power.

The Savior enters rooms of grief and restores. Arise is both gift and call into renewed life.
verses.reformedNotes:
Authority clears the room, then raises the dead by hand. Narrative economy matches divine ease.

The girl’s arising previews greater resurrection hope secured in Christ.

verses.text: The report of this went out into all that land.
verses.arminianNotes:
News spreads. Mercy refuses to stay secret for long. Testimony invites others to seek the same Lord.

Let the report reach you as summons—come to Jesus with death-sized needs.
verses.reformedNotes:
Providence multiplies witness through the district. Fame serves the kingdom’s advance under the Father’s plan.

Report is not chaos; it prepares ears for the King.
